title: How Plants Reproduce
hook: Flowers aren't just decoration — they're how most plants have sex, trading pollen so they can pack the next generation into seeds that travel.
key_points: In flowering plants, flowers are the reproductive organs.
Pollination moves pollen (male cells) to the female part of a flower.
Fertilized flowers develop seeds, often wrapped in fruit that aids dispersal.
Wind, water, insects, and other animals all act as pollinators.
Some plants, like ferns and mosses, reproduce with spores instead of seeds.
content_html: For most plants, reproduction runs through the flower. A flower is the plant's sexual organ, holding both pollen (the male cells) and the female parts that contain eggs. Pollination is the hand-off: pollen has to travel from one flower's male part to another's female part, carried by wind, water, or animals like bees. Once an egg is fertilized, the flower transforms — its ovules become seeds, and the surrounding tissue often swells into fruit.
extra_html: That fruit is a clever trick: by wrapping seeds in something sweet or sticky or feathery, a plant gets animals and weather to carry its offspring far from the parent, where there's room and light to grow. This is why so many plants invest in bright petals and nectar — they're advertising to pollinators. But flowers and seeds aren't the only way. Older plant lineages like ferns and mosses skip seeds entirely and reproduce with spores, single cells that drift off and grow into new plants. As Khan Academy's overview of plant reproduction lays out, the leap to flowers and seeds was a major evolutionary upgrade that helped flowering plants dominate the land.

related.title: How a Plant Is Built
related.hook: Most plants are made of three working parts — roots that drink, stems that lift, and leaves that catch sunlight — and together they turn dirt and light into a living thing.

related.title: Why Plants Run the Planet
related.hook: Nearly every breath you take and every meal you eat traces back to plants — they make the oxygen, anchor the food chain, and lock away carbon for the whole biosphere.

flashcards.back_html: The transfer of pollen (carrying male cells) to the female part of a flower. Once pollen reaches the egg, fertilization can occur and a seed can form.

flashcards.prompt: What develops from a flower after it is fertilized?

choices.text: Seeds, often enclosed in a fruit

flashcards.explanation_html: Fertilization turns the flower's ovules into seeds, and the surrounding tissue often becomes a fruit that helps carry those seeds away from the parent plant.

flashcards.prompt: How do ferns and mosses reproduce, unlike flowering plants?

choices.text: By growing flowers with extra pollen

flashcards.explanation_html: Ferns and mosses are seedless plants — they scatter tiny spores instead of producing flowers and seeds.
